The majority voted against a motion to amend the usual [second reading motion](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html), which is that the majority should agree with the main idea of the [bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6256) (or, in parliamentary jargon, that the majority should agree to read the bill for a second time). Since this motion was unsuccessful, the original motion will remain unchanged and [can be voted on as is](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/divisions/representatives/2018-12-06/3). ### Motion text > *That all words after “That” be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *“the House declines to give the bill a second reading, and notes:* > *(1) this unprecedented intervention into markets which will result in higher prices for families and businesses;* > *(2) the Government has abandoned all pretence at being the party of free enterprise and open markets; and* > *(3) the Government has abandoned all proper process, scrutiny and consultation.”* ### What is the main idea of the bill? This bill is part of the Government's package of measures in relation to the electricity sector. For example, the bill sets out three kinds of prohibited conduct in relation to retail prices, the electricity financial contract market and the wholesale electricity market. The remedies included in the bill are graduated, from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) issuing a public warning notice to the ACCC applying to a court for a pecuniary penalty. The bill also gives new compulsory information gathering powers on the Australian Energy Regulator (AER) and lets the AER share information with other agencies. The Labor Party was concerned with the [speed this legislation](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2018-12-05.125.2) was being pushed through Parliament by the Coalition Government.

The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to resume debate on the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, arguing that passing it within 48 hours would allow Senate passage by February 2019 and force energy companies to lower electricity prices, while delay would push passage to at least April 2019.

The speaker argued that Labor opposes the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 to protect big energy company profits, citing an ACCC finding that three players control 80% of dispatchable generation. They claimed Labor's 45% emission reduction target requires higher electricity prices and will wreck the economy, also tightening rules on farmers' land.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, which creates prohibitions on retail pricing, contract liquidity, and wholesale bid misconduct to lower electricity costs. The bill establishes a graduated enforcement process—including warning notices, civil penalties up to $10 million or 10% of turnover, and divestment as a last resort—citing ACCC evidence of market dysfunction and price discrepancies such as $411–$832 annual differences for households.

The speaker argued that the government rushed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 through parliament without proper scrutiny, calling the process chaotic and unacceptable. They criticised the government’s energy policy as a "dog's breakfast" and "harebrained," noting it was the tenth iteration, lacked expert support, and included an unprecedented and possibly unconstitutional divestiture power not recommended by ACCC chairman Rod Sims.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, arguing that divestiture powers for the ACCC should extend to all markets, not just energy, to address abuses such as supermarkets squeezing agricultural suppliers. The speaker credited former senator Nick Xenophon for championing this power and noted that the court, not a minister, should have the final say on divestiture as a remedy of last resort.

The speaker argued the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 would penalise energy companies for misconduct with graduated penalties including divestiture, and criticised the Queensland Labor government for maintaining an effective monopoly, overinvesting $7.3 billion in poles and wires, imposing a six per cent guaranteed return, and failing to pass on a 40 per cent wholesale price reduction to consumers.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 was condemned as the worst, shallowest, and most ill-conceived legislation seen in the parliament, being rushed, unsupported by any inquiry or the ACCC, and opposed by business groups—argued to fail in reducing electricity prices, increase carbon emissions, deter investment, and destroy jobs.

The bill would take effect when the main merger act starts, and it preserves existing judicial appointments and handles appeals already filed at that date.
The bill amends the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 to create the Family Law Appeal Division.
The bill amends the Family Law Act 1975 so it works with the new court structure.
The bill removes most of the Family Court’s appellate function and gives it to the Federal Court’s new division.
The bill provides a framework to transition the titles and appointments of judges and other personnel from the Family Court and the Federal Circuit Court to the new divisions.
The bill sets transitional arrangements for family law appeals that are ongoing or eligible to be filed when the new court starts.
The bill ensures that any first-instance cases already in the Family Court or Federal Circuit Court continue in the corresponding new division.

Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2018 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

The bill merges the Family Court of Australia and the Federal Circuit Court of Australia into a single Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, creating a unified administrative structure and a new family law appeal division in the Federal Court, aiming to resolve disputes more quickly and efficiently while addressing a backlog of 21,000 pending cases and rising median trial times.

The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2018 establishes a new Family Law Appeal Division in the Federal Court from 1 January 2019, transferring most Family Court appellate functions to that division and providing $4 million for harmonising court rules.

Labor opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 and related bill, citing no stakeholder consultation, insufficient evidence for clearing 8,000 extra cases, and concerns that the merger would effectively abolish the specialist Family Court by attrition, with appeals heard by a single Federal Court judge lacking family law experience.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018, arguing it would gradually abolish the specialist Family Court by merging it with the Federal Circuit Court, halting new appointments to Division 1, and transferring appellate jurisdiction to the Federal Court. They criticised inadequate consultation with stakeholders, reliance on a PricewaterhouseCoopers report, and the government's failure to properly resource the Family Court, which they said caused the backlogs the bill purportedly addresses.

The speaker opposed the bills merging the Family Court of Australia into the Federal Circuit Court, arguing the government rushed the process without consulting stakeholders or awaiting the Australian Law Reform Commission’s report, and that the true cause of delays is inadequate resourcing—not court structure—pointing to the Family Court of Western Australia having only five judges, unchanged since 1975 despite population growth.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018, arguing it would abolish the family law system by stealth rather than fix under-resourcing, and called for adequate funding of courts and legal aid instead of amalgamation.

Labor will oppose the proposed merger of the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court, arguing it would eliminate specialist family-law expertise and endanger domestic-violence victims while providing zero additional funding—despite backlogs growing from 17,000 to 21,000 cases and median trial times rising to 15.2 and 17 months.

The speaker argued that the government's plan to merge the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court, through the two bills, was based on a rushed six-week desktop review by PwC and a three-week consultation period for a 500-page bill, with virtually no input from experts or the sector, and would eliminate specialist family law expertise, prioritising speed and cost over the best outcomes for children and families. They noted that the Law Council and other bodies opposed the changes, only two government members spoke on the bills, and a Law Reform Commission review was due in March 2019.

The speaker supported the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 to merge the two family courts, citing current wait times exceeding 15 months and cases taking up to five years, and claimed the merger would finalise an additional 3,000 cases per year and eliminate 35,000 cases being referred to the wrong court.

The speaker argued that the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 merges the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court into a single structure without abolishing the Family Court, creates a new family law appeal division in the Federal Court, and delays the commencement date due to a Senate inquiry. The government allocated $4 million for implementation and predicted $3 million in savings to be reinvested, aiming to reduce waiting times and improve case management.
The bill would merge the Federal Circuit Court and the Family Court into a single administrative structure called the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia.
The new court would have two divisions, with one Chief Justice holding a dual commission to both divisions, and would create a consistent case management approach for family law matters.
The bill would not allow decided family law matters to be reopened based on these reforms alone.
Creates the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia as an overarching administrative structure.

Confers family law jurisdiction on both divisions under the Family Law Act 1975.
Allows matters to be transferred between divisions with the approval of the receiving division's Chief Justice or Chief Judge.
Requires the Chief Justice and Chief Judge to work cooperatively on common case management approaches.

The speaker supported the government's drug-testing trial for 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, arguing it would identify and help welfare recipients with substance abuse through income management and treatment, with refusal resulting in loss of benefits.

They cited local support, a $10 million boost for drug treatment services, and existing government investments in Mandurah including $2 million for a youth health hub, $581 million for the Tonkin Highway extension, and a drop in unemployment from 11.6% to 6.5%.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is arbitrary, cruel, and lacks evidence, and that drug addiction should be treated as a health issue rather than a punitive measure. They noted the trial would randomly test 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients, with payment cancellation for refusal, and cited opposition from medical experts and community organisations, as well as long waits for rehabilitation.

Labor opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is based on flawed assumptions and would harm vulnerable people. The speaker argued for the drug testing trial in the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, describing it as a non-punitive, world-leading measure to break intergenerational welfare dependency and drug addiction, citing 83% coalition voter support and 65% Labor voter support, and referencing the $685 million national ice initiative and $10 million for trial areas.

Centre Alliance maintained its opposition to the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it is a rebadged version of a previously rejected bill with no published costings, and citing US evidence that such programs are ineffective and expensive. The party called on parliament to again reject the legislation, stating that existing addiction services are underfunded and that the bill is a populist attempt to demonise welfare recipients.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2018, arguing it would drive up crime and demonise welfare recipients, citing the opposition of a former Australian Federal Police commissioner and the lack of any credible expert support.

The bill introduces a two-year drug testing trial for 5,000 new Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, with income management for positive tests and a $10 million treatment fund. The speaker argued the trial identifies jobseekers with drug abuse issues and helps them access treatment and employment.

Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 - Consideration in Detail - Agree with bill

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 was introduced to reduce regulatory burden by removing the five-voyage minimum for temporary licences, relaxing tolerance provisions, simplifying consultation requirements, and extending coverage to floating production storage and offloading units and dry-docking vessels. The bill aims to address the expected 30% growth in Australia's freight task by 2030, with coastal shipping currently projected to increase only 15%.

The 2012 Coastal Trading Act failed to halt the decline of Australian shipping, and the 2017 amendment bill should be passed to allow foreign superyachts to charter in Australia by removing customs import duties, which could create 11,800 jobs and $1.64 billion in economic benefit by 2021.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would allow foreign vessels to dominate Australian coastal trade, undermine Australian jobs and wages, and cited that the 2015 bill's regulatory impact statement predicted 1,000 of 1,100 maritime workers would be sacked. They highlighted opposition from the Maritime Union of Australia, Maritime Industry Australia Limited, and the Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers, and referenced the MV Portland and CSL Melbourne incidents where Australian crews were replaced by foreign crews.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would benefit their electorate of Fisher by boosting tourism and economic activity through relaxed superyacht regulations. They cited potential growth in GDP contributions from $590 million to $3.34 billion by 2021 and 8,100 additional jobs, with specific reference to the Mooloolaba Spit and Browns Slipway.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 will decimate seafaring jobs and the maritime industry in Australia. The speaker waited 11 weeks through a gruelling by-election campaign to speak on this bill.

The bill would cause hundreds of Australian seafarer job losses, particularly in Tasmania, by allowing foreign ships and crews to replace Australian vessels on coastal routes, and was developed without consulting the peak shipping industry body, Maritime Industry Australia Ltd.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would accelerate the decline of Australia's merchant fleet and harm national security, environmental protection, and jobs—noting that 12 Australian-flagged vessels have been reflagged under the current government and that the bill's regulatory impact statement explicitly aims to remove barriers for foreign vessels.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 should be passed to remove customs duties and taxes on superyachts, allow temporary licences for round trips, and enable charters, which would generate $1.64 billion and create nearly 12,000 jobs, particularly in Queensland regions like the Whitsundays, Bowen, and Cairns.

The speaker argued against the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, accusing the Liberal Party of seeking to decimate Australian coastal shipping by replacing Australian vessels, workers, and wages with foreign ones. They specifically criticised the member for Dawson for advocating GST removal on vessels worth $100 million while ordinary Australians still pay GST.

The speech opposed the Turnbull government's Coastal Trading Bill, arguing it would destroy Australia's remaining shipping industry and seafarer jobs while favouring foreign vessels, and supported Labor's amendment. It cited the decline to just 12 Australian coastal trading vessels, the Port of Newcastle's 4,600 annual ship movements, and an ACCC investigation into the NSW port privatisation deal.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would decimate Australian shipping jobs and industry, citing that 93% of Australian seafarers could be replaced, over 1,000 jobs lost, and 88% of savings from cheap foreign labour, and criticised changes to tolerance limits and licence variation processes.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would destroy Australian shipping jobs by allowing foreign flag-of-convenience vessels to undercut Australian wages and safety standards, and noted opposition from industry bodies including the Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers, Maritime Industry Australia Ltd, and the Maritime Union of Australia. The speaker also referenced the Howard government's illegal lockout of maritime workers in 1998 as part of a pattern of undermining Australian maritime jobs.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would accelerate the decline of Australia's shipping industry, citing the loss of 12 Australian-flagged vessels since 2013, including the MV Portland. They opposed the bill’s tolerance provisions and licence variation changes, claiming they would disadvantage Australian vessels and workers while favouring foreign operators with lower wages.

The speaker argued that the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 would further deregulate and destroy Australia's shipping industry, reducing the fleet from hundreds of vessels in the 1980s to only 11 or 12 today. They claimed this creates national security risks, economic harm, and labour exploitation, citing the loss of Australian-crewed oil tankers, reliance on foreign vessels for fuel, and the live sheep export trade as examples, while opposing the bill in favour of a long-term strategy to revitalise the industry.

The speaker opposed the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it would weaken the regulatory framework, harm Australian seafarers, and reduce sovereign self-sufficiency; they noted that Australian flagged ships declined from 55 in 1996 to 21 in 2007 under the Howard government and that no Australian general licensed vessel currently can transport petroleum.

The MP supported the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 but expressed significant concerns about measures including increasing cargo volume tolerance from ±20% to +200%/−100%, expanding loading date tolerance from 5 to 30 days, and halving the time for Australian vessels to apply for temporary licences from 48 hours to 24 hours, arguing these would harm the coastal shipping sector. They also flagged concern over extending the regime to chartered recreational vessels, reserving their party's final position.

The speaker called on the government to withdraw the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, arguing it is designed to cut Australian jobs and wages by making it easier for shipowners to replace Australian-flagged vessels and crews with foreign ones. They cited the loss of the Iron Chieftain at Port Kembla, warned of risks to national security and the environment, and criticised the government for dismantling previous Labor reforms that had aimed to rebuild the shipping industry.

Opposing the Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017, the member for Brand argued it should be withdrawn, citing official modelling that 93 per cent of Australian seafarer jobs would be lost and criticising the government for inadequate consultation. She supported amendments by the member for Grayndler and the member for Whitlam, and defended Labor's 2012 coastal trading reforms against what she described as a repeat of the coalition's failed 2015 attempt.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 was argued to be necessary to reverse the decline of Australia's shipping fleet and workforce caused by decades of neoliberal policies, and to instead use regulation and tax arrangements to increase employment, safety, environmental protection, and revenue.

The Coastal Trading (Revitalising Australian Shipping) Amendment Bill 2017 simplifies coastal trading regulation, removes the five-voyage minimum for temporary licences, expands coverage to offshore petroleum and superyachts, and reduces red tape to boost efficiency, fuel security, and tourism.
Corporations Amendment (Asia Region Funds Passport) Bill 2018

The Corporations Amendment (Asia Region Funds Passport) Bill 2018 implements a regulatory framework to remove duplicated barriers for qualifying managed funds, with Australia holding A$3 trillion in funds under management but only 4% sourced from overseas, compared to 69% in Hong Kong and 80% in Singapore. Participating economies are Japan, Korea, New Zealand, and Thailand.

The government introduced the Customs Amendment (Anti-Dumping Measures) Bill 2017 to close a loophole where foreign exporters could limit exports during duty reviews to obtain lower rates and resume dumping. The bill gives the Anti-Dumping Commission three specific methods to set export prices when exporters have made no or unrepresentative exports during a review period, protecting Australian manufacturers and jobs.
Australian Border Force Amendment (Protected Information) Bill 2017

The Australian Border Force Amendment (Protected Information) Bill 2017 clarifies part 6 of the Australian Border Force Act to prevent unauthorised disclosure of information harmful to national or public interest, while allowing appropriate disclosure, with retrospective application to 2015.

The government moved amendments to the Australian Border Force Amendment (Protected Information) Bill 2017 to replace the secretary with the minister as the authority to prescribe additional kinds of "immigration and border protection information" by legislative instrument, addressing concerns about an unelected official exercising this power.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Enterprise Tax Plan No. 2) Bill 2017

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Enterprise Tax Plan No. 2) Bill 2017 and opposed the amendment, arguing corporate tax cuts are needed for competitiveness and job creation. He criticised the Shadow Treasurer for abandoning his past support for lower company tax rates, citing the UK’s cuts to 23 per cent in April 2013 and 21 per cent in April 2014, and accused Labor of waging a war on business with no job-creating policies.
ASIC Supervisory Cost Recovery Levy Bill 2017

The ASIC Supervisory Cost Recovery Levy Bill 2017 introduces an industry funding model to make regulated entities pay for ASIC's costs, shifting the burden from taxpayers. The bill also grants ASIC enforcement powers including penalty interest and licence suspension, building on a $127.2 million funding package from 2016.
Hazardous Waste (Regulation of Exports and Imports) Amendment Bill 2016

The bill introduces administrative efficiency reforms and cost recovery measures for hazardous waste permit schemes, shifting costs from taxpayers to waste movers by raising permit fees and imposing an indexed levy.
Competition and Consumer Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2016

The Competition and Consumer Amendment (Country of Origin) Bill 2016 was introduced to simplify and clarify safe harbour provisions in Australian consumer law, as part of a government reform package agreed by states and territories in March 2016, with the Country of Origin Food Labelling Information Standard 2016 having commenced in July 2016.
